bad: Today we will look how the method works.
good: Today, we’ll look at how the method works.
why: “Look” needs the preposition “at” before the thing you examine. The phrase “look at how…” introduces an explanation naturally; “we’ll” is a common spoken contraction for opening a lesson or talk.
story: I was introducing a new topic in a small seminar.
The students had read a short overview before class.
I put the first diagram on the screen and said, “Today, we’ll look at how the method works.”
I explained the main steps and paused at each part of the diagram.
A student asked how the second step differed from the baseline.
We used that question to begin the discussion.

bad: Do you have any question until now?
good: Any questions so far?
why: “Any questions so far?” is a concise, natural check for questions up to this point in a lesson or presentation. “So far” expresses “until now,” and “questions” is plural when you are inviting any questions from the group.
story: I had just finished explaining the first part of a new topic.
Several students were taking notes, and one person looked uncertain.
I paused and asked, “Any questions so far?”
A student asked me to go over one of the terms again.
I gave a simpler example and checked that the distinction was clear.
Then we continued to the next section.

bad: Let’s move next example.
good: Let’s move on to the next example.
why: The usual expression for changing to a new topic or item is “move on to.” It takes “to” before the next topic, and “the” identifies the next example in the sequence.
story: We had worked through two examples on the board.
The class understood the first one but wanted another case.
I said, “Let’s move on to the next example.”
I brought up a new problem that used the same principle.
The students compared it with the earlier example in pairs.
We discussed where the two cases behaved differently.

bad: The point what I want to explain is the results are different.
good: The key point is that the two results differ.
why: The original combines two sentence structures, which makes the main claim difficult to follow. “The key point is that…” clearly introduces one complete idea, and “differ” states the comparison directly.
story: I was summarizing two results during a group presentation.
The values looked similar at first glance, but the trend changed across datasets.
I highlighted the chart and said, “The key point is that the two results differ.”
I pointed to the cases where the difference was largest.
A colleague asked whether the same pattern appeared in the smaller dataset.
We checked the table together before drawing a conclusion.

bad: This figure is comparing between two methods.
good: This figure compares the two methods.
why: A figure does not perform the act of comparing; it presents information that lets the audience compare the methods. “Compare” takes the two items directly, so “between” is unnecessary here.
story: I was preparing a slide for our weekly lab meeting.
The figure showed the performance of two approaches across four tasks.
I introduced it by saying, “This figure compares the two methods.”
I explained what each color represented before discussing the results.
The team noticed that one method improved on only two tasks.
We added a note to make that limitation clear on the slide.

bad: I’ll stop for question here.
good: I’ll pause here for questions.
why: “Pause here” is a natural way to signal a temporary break in a talk, and “for questions” names why you are stopping. Use plural “questions” when inviting the audience to ask anything.
story: I had just finished the first half of a short presentation.
The audience had been following a few technical details on the slides.
I said, “I’ll pause here for questions.”
One person asked how we selected the evaluation set.
I answered briefly and offered to explain the details after the talk.
Then I continued with the results section.

bad: Let me explain again in other way.
good: Let me rephrase that.
why: “Rephrase” means to express the same idea in different words, so it is a concise fit when someone did not understand an explanation. The original is understandable, but “in another way” would be the grammatical form if you wanted to describe the method more literally.
story: I was explaining a result during office hours.
A student understood the calculation but not why we used that step.
I stopped and said, “Let me rephrase that.”
I described the same idea with an example from everyday life.
The student connected it to the equation on the page.
We moved on once the reasoning was clear.

bad: Do you understand until now?
good: Does that make sense so far?
why: “Does that make sense so far?” checks whether the explanation is clear without putting one listener on the spot to prove they understand. “So far” is the natural phrase for checking progress up to the current point.
story: I was teaching a new procedure in a workshop.
After a few steps, I noticed that some participants had stopped writing.
I paused and asked, “Does that make sense so far?”
One person said they were unsure about the second step.
I demonstrated it again with a smaller example.
The group continued once everyone had the sequence in their notes.

bad: Let’s look more close to the final step.
good: Let’s take a closer look at the final step.
why: The fixed phrase is “take a closer look at”; “closer” is the comparative adjective that modifies “look.” Use “at” to introduce the part you want the audience to examine.
story: The class had followed a procedure through most of its stages.
The last step was where several groups made different choices.
I said, “Let’s take a closer look at the final step.”
I enlarged that part of the diagram on the screen.
We compared the two choices and traced their effects.
The students then revised their own solutions.

bad: To summary, the model works better on small datasets.
good: To summarize, the model performs better on small datasets.
why: After “to,” use the verb “summarize,” not the noun “summary.” “Performs better” is also a precise way to describe a model’s measured results; explain which datasets or metric support the comparison when you present it.
story: I was wrapping up a presentation about our evaluation.
The audience had seen the results for several dataset sizes.
I said, “To summarize, the model performs better on small datasets.”
I showed the metric that supported the comparison.
A listener asked whether the same trend held for the largest dataset.
I noted that we needed more evaluation before making a broader claim.

bad: I will explain about my update first.
good: I’ll start with a brief update.
why: “Explain about” is not the usual pattern; “explain” takes its topic directly, while “give an update” and “start with an update” are natural meeting phrases. “Brief” signals that you will keep the opening concise.
story: Our lab meeting began with a quick round of updates.
I had finished one experiment and was starting another.
I opened by saying, “I’ll start with a brief update.”
I summarized what had changed since the previous week.
Then I showed one result that raised a new question.
The group helped me decide what to test next.

bad: From our last meeting, I did two experiments.
good: Since our last meeting, I’ve run two experiments.
why: “Since our last meeting” marks a period that began then and continues up to now, so the present perfect “I’ve run” fits a progress update. “Run an experiment” is the standard collocation in research contexts.
story: I was preparing a short update for our weekly meeting.
The team wanted to know what had changed since we last spoke.
I said, “Since our last meeting, I’ve run two experiments.”
I showed the setup and summarized the results of each one.
One run revealed an unexpected difference between the datasets.
We agreed to investigate that difference before the next meeting.

bad: I met a problem with the training run.
good: I ran into an issue with the training run.
why: English speakers say “run into an issue/problem” when they encounter an unexpected difficulty. “Met a problem” is a direct translation that is not idiomatic in this context; “issue” also keeps the tone neutral for a meeting update.
story: The training job stopped earlier than expected overnight.
I checked the logs before our morning group meeting.
I told the team, “I ran into an issue with the training run.”
I showed the error message and explained what I had already tried.
A teammate recognized a similar problem from a previous experiment.
We made a small configuration change and restarted the job.

bad: These result is not final yet.
good: These results are preliminary.
why: “Results” is plural, so it takes “are,” not “is.” “Preliminary” is a concise academic word for findings that are early and may change after more analysis; use it to avoid presenting them as final.
story: I had completed the first pass of an evaluation.
Some runs were still missing, so the table was not complete.
At the meeting, I said, “These results are preliminary.”
I explained which experiments had finished and which were still running.
The group suggested a check for one unusual value.
I added that check to the analysis plan.

bad: Could we discuss about the next steps?
good: Could we discuss the next steps?
why: “Discuss” takes the topic as a direct object, so it is followed by “the next steps” without “about.” If you want to keep “about,” use “Could we talk about the next steps?” instead.
story: We had reviewed the latest results and written down two possible follow-up experiments.
The meeting was nearly over, and we needed to agree on what to do first.
I asked, “Could we discuss the next steps?”
My advisor suggested prioritizing the experiment that would answer our main question.
We divided the tasks and set a date to check in.
I added the plan to our shared notes.

bad: I want your feedback for this analysis.
good: I’d appreciate your feedback on this analysis.
why: Use “feedback on” when naming the work you want someone to review. “I want your feedback” is clear but can sound demanding in a meeting; “I’d appreciate…” makes it a courteous request while keeping the request specific.
story: I had drafted an analysis plan for the new dataset.
Before running every experiment, I wanted a second opinion on the comparison.
I asked my advisor, “I’d appreciate your feedback on this analysis.”
I pointed out the assumptions I was least certain about.
They suggested one additional baseline and a clearer description of the metric.
I revised the plan before beginning the full evaluation.

bad: What are the takeaway points from this result?
good: What are the main takeaways from this result?
why: “Takeaway” already means the main point to remember, so “takeaway points” is usually redundant. “Main takeaways” is a natural way to ask the group to identify the most important implications of a result.
story: We had just finished reviewing a long set of evaluation tables.
Several metrics moved in different directions across the tasks.
I asked, “What are the main takeaways from this result?”
One teammate pointed out a consistent improvement on the smaller datasets.
Another noted that the gains disappeared for the largest task.
We wrote down both observations for the next draft.

bad: What means this part of the paper?
good: Could you clarify what this part of the paper means?
why: In a present simple question, use “does” before the subject and keep the main verb in its base form (“What does this mean?”). “Could you clarify…” is a more collaborative way to ask about a passage during a research discussion.
story: We were reading a paper together before the group meeting.
A paragraph described an assumption that was not obvious to me.
I asked, “Could you clarify what this part of the paper means?”
A colleague paraphrased the claim and pointed to the definition above it.
We checked how the authors used the term in the next section.
The passage made more sense once we connected the two parts.

bad: I couldn’t understand the last step.
good: I’m not sure I follow the last step.
why: The original is grammatical, but it can sound like a blunt judgment of the explanation. “I’m not sure I follow…” frames the difficulty as a request for clarification and is a common, tactful phrase in meetings.
story: A teammate walked us through a derivation on the whiteboard.
The first few steps were familiar, but the final transition was quick.
I said, “I’m not sure I follow the last step.”
They rewrote the equation and explained which assumption they used.
I asked one more question about the variable substitution.
Then I could see how the result followed from the earlier line.

bad: We have delay in the project.
good: We’re slightly behind schedule.
why: “Behind schedule” is the usual phrase for work that is taking longer than planned. “Slightly” gives a measured update; name the cause and revised date if the team needs to make a new plan.
story: Our team had planned to finish the annotation by Thursday.
A few files needed extra review, so the work was taking longer than expected.
I updated the group by saying, “We’re slightly behind schedule.”
I explained which part needed more time and gave a revised estimate.
The team moved one internal review to the following week.
We updated the shared timeline before ending the meeting.

bad: Next slide shows the main result.
good: The next slide shows the main result.
why: Use “the” because you mean the particular slide that follows in this presentation. The simple present “shows” is natural when describing what a slide, figure, or table contains.
story: I was rehearsing the transition between the methods and results sections.
The audience would have seen several setup slides before this point.
I said, “The next slide shows the main result.”
Then I brought up the chart and explained its axes.
I highlighted the comparison that answered our research question.
The transition helped the audience see why the result mattered.

bad: We will discuss more detail later.
good: We’ll discuss this in more detail later.
why: The natural phrase is “in more detail,” and the audience needs an object such as “this” to show what you will return to. This wording signals that the current slide gives only a brief overview.
story: I was giving a short overview of a complicated evaluation setup.
The audience needed the main idea before seeing all the details.
I said, “We’ll discuss this in more detail later.”
I moved on to the result that depended on the setup.
Near the end, I returned to the evaluation choices and answered questions.
The audience had enough context to follow the deeper explanation.

bad: I will share you the slides after presentation.
good: I’ll share the slides after the presentation.
why: “Share” takes the thing being shared as its object; use “with” before the recipient (“share the slides with you”). “After the presentation” takes “the” when referring to the specific talk you have just given.
story: I had presented our early findings at a department seminar.
A few people asked for the charts so they could review them later.
I told the audience, “I’ll share the slides after the presentation.”
After the questions, I checked the file for the latest figures.
I sent the deck to the attendees with a short note.
Several colleagues replied with useful comments the next day.

bad: Thank you for listening my presentation.
good: Thanks for your attention.
why: “Listen” takes “to” before the thing you listen to, but “Thanks for your attention” is the conventional concise closing for a presentation. You can also say “Thank you for listening to my presentation” when you specifically want to mention listening.
story: I had reached the final slide after presenting our study.
The audience had followed the methods and results and asked several questions.
I closed by saying, “Thanks for your attention.”
The session chair thanked me and invited the audience to continue the discussion.
A few people came over afterward to ask about the dataset.
I shared the paper link with them before leaving the room.

bad: The algorithm receives in input and gives output.
good: The algorithm takes an input and returns an output.
why: English commonly says an algorithm “takes an input” and “returns an output.” These verb–noun pairings are standard in technical explanations; “receive as input” is also natural, but “receive in input” is not the usual construction.
story: I was introducing a search algorithm during our lab presentation.
The audience had seen the problem statement but not the implementation.
I began with, “The algorithm takes an input and returns an output.”
Then I named the input structure and described what the output represents.
A slide showed how the first transformation prepares the data.
The team could follow the rest of the explanation from that starting point.

bad: First, we divide the input to tokens.
good: First, we split the input into tokens.
why: Use “split something into parts” when describing how one item is divided into smaller units. “Tokens” is plural because the operation usually produces multiple units; “divide” can also work with “into,” but “split into tokens” is the usual concise phrasing here.
story: I was explaining the preprocessing stage of a language model.
The first slide showed a sentence before and after tokenization.
I said, “First, we split the input into tokens.”
Then I explained how each token receives an ID.
The next diagram showed those IDs moving into the model.
The audience could see where the later computations begin.

bad: We repeat this step until the loss will converge.
good: We repeat this step until the loss converges.
why: In a time or condition clause introduced by “until,” use the present simple for a future event: “until the loss converges.” The main clause can still describe the repeated action; the extra “will” is not used in this standard pattern.
story: I was describing the training loop in a methods talk.
The audience wanted to know how long the optimization continues.
I explained, “We repeat this step until the loss converges.”
A plot showed the loss decreasing over successive updates.
I noted that in practice we also stop at a preset limit.
That distinction helped clarify the procedure and its implementation.

bad: The algorithm runs in O(n) time complexity.
good: The algorithm runs in linear time.
why: “Runs in linear time” is a concise verbal description of O(n) time complexity. The original is understandable, but “in O(n) time complexity” combines two ways of naming the same property; use the concise phrase in speech and give the formal notation on the slide if useful.
story: I was comparing two algorithms for processing a large list.
One audience member asked how their running times differ as the list grows.
I said, “The algorithm runs in linear time.”
Then I wrote O(n) next to the pseudocode.
We discussed how the number of operations changes with input size.
The notation and the spoken explanation described the same growth rate.

bad: The runtime increases linear as the input grows.
good: The runtime grows linearly with the input size.
why: Use the adverb “linearly” to describe how the runtime grows, and “with” to connect that growth to input size. This phrasing states the relationship clearly without claiming an exact runtime for every input.
story: Our team was discussing how the method scales to larger datasets.
The runtime plot showed a steady increase as the inputs grew.
I summarized the trend by saying, “The runtime grows linearly with the input size.”
I pointed to the axes and clarified how we measured each run.
A colleague asked whether the same pattern held for longer sequences.
We added that case to the next round of experiments.

bad: We evaluate the model in three benchmarks.
good: We evaluate the model on three benchmarks.
why: English usually uses “evaluate a model on a benchmark or dataset” to name the test set. “In” is used for a setting or environment (“in a low-resource setting”), while “on” introduces the benchmark used for evaluation.
story: I was presenting the evaluation setup for our new model.
The audience needed to know which tasks were included.
I said, “We evaluate the model on three benchmarks.”
I named each benchmark and briefly described its test split.
One reviewer asked whether all methods used the same data.
I showed the shared evaluation protocol on the next slide.

bad: We compare our results with baseline.
good: We compare our results with the baseline.
why: Use “the baseline” when you mean the specific reference method in the experiment; the singular countable noun needs a determiner. “Compare our results with” is a natural way to describe the evaluation, and “against” is another common option.
story: I was walking the group through the main evaluation table.
The baseline appeared in the first row for reference.
I said, “We compare our results with the baseline.”
Then I explained the metric and pointed out the largest difference.
A colleague asked whether the baseline had the same training budget.
We checked the experiment settings before interpreting the result.

bad: This module is in charge to parse input.
good: This module handles input parsing.
why: “In charge” is followed by “of,” not “to,” and it usually describes responsibility assigned to a person or team. For a software component, “handles input parsing” is concise and directly names the component’s function.
story: I was explaining the architecture of a data-processing pipeline.
Each box in the diagram represented a separate software module.
I pointed to the first box and said, “This module handles input parsing.”
I described how it checks the incoming format before passing data onward.
The next component performs normalization and validation.
The separation makes each part easier to test independently.

bad: The data is flowing from parser to planner.
good: The data flows from the parser to the planner.
why: Use the simple present to describe a stable process or a data-flow diagram. “The parser” and “the planner” refer to specific components, so they take “the”; the continuous form would emphasize data moving at this moment.
story: I showed a diagram of the system’s main components.
The audience asked how a request moves through the pipeline.
I traced the arrows and said, “The data flows from the parser to the planner.”
I explained what information each component adds.
Then I showed where the planner sends its result.
The diagram made the handoff between components easier to understand.

bad: The design separates retrieval and generation into different.
good: The design separates retrieval from generation.
why: The verb “separate” commonly takes the pattern “separate A from B.” The shorter alternative names the two stages directly; add “into two stages” if you want to emphasize the resulting structure.
story: I was introducing a two-stage system for a paper discussion.
The first stage finds documents, and the second produces a response.
I summarized the architecture by saying, “The design separates retrieval from generation.”
A diagram showed the output of one stage becoming the input to the next.
We discussed how this structure makes each stage easier to evaluate.
I also noted that the stages still depend on each other’s outputs.

bad: The main bottleneck locates in the database lookup.
good: The main bottleneck is the database lookup.
why: “Bottleneck” names the component or operation that limits performance, so a linking verb such as “is” connects it to the cause. “Is located” describes physical position; it does not fit as naturally when identifying which operation slows the system.
story: We profiled the service after response times began to increase.
The trace showed that one operation took much longer than the others.
At the meeting, I said, “The main bottleneck is the database lookup.”
I showed the timing breakdown and explained how we measured it.
A teammate suggested checking whether the cache was being used.
We added that measurement to the next profiling run.

bad: This assumption is held in small graph but not dense one.
good: This assumption holds for small graphs, but not for dense ones.
why: “Hold” means remain valid in this context, so use the active form “the assumption holds.” “For” introduces the cases where it applies, and plural “graphs” and “ones” refer to the class of graphs being discussed.
story: I was explaining an assumption behind our graph algorithm.
The method behaved differently as the graph became denser.
I clarified, “This assumption holds for small graphs, but not for dense ones.”
I showed two examples with different edge densities.
A student asked what happens near the transition point.
We discussed how to test that boundary in a follow-up experiment.

bad: The method is sensitive with choosing the threshold.
good: The method is sensitive to the choice of threshold.
why: The adjective “sensitive” is followed by “to” when naming the factor that affects a method. “The choice of threshold” makes clear that the result may change depending on which threshold is selected.
story: We tested the method with several threshold values.
The scores changed more than we had expected.
I noted, “The method is sensitive to the choice of threshold.”
I showed the range of results rather than reporting only the best value.
My advisor asked whether the threshold could be selected on validation data.
We added that question to our evaluation plan.

bad: Our implement uses caching for avoid repeat computation.
good: Our implementation uses caching to avoid repeated computation.
why: “Implementation” is the noun for the code or realized system; “implement” is a verb. Use “to avoid” to express purpose, and “repeated computation” is the natural noun phrase for work that would otherwise be done again.
story: I was describing an optimization in our prototype.
The system often requested the same intermediate result more than once.
I explained, “Our implementation uses caching to avoid repeated computation.”
I showed how the cache stores the result for later requests.
The team asked whether it changed memory use.
I added a small table comparing runtime and memory for both settings.

bad: We can make same result with this configuration.
good: We can reproduce the result with this configuration.
why: In research, “reproduce a result” means obtain the same finding by following a specified procedure or setup. “Make the same result” is not the usual collocation; naming the configuration helps others understand what they need to repeat.
story: A collaborator wanted to verify a result from our earlier run.
I shared the configuration file and the version of the dataset.
I explained, “We can reproduce the result with this configuration.”
They ran the experiment on their machine that afternoon.
The score was close to ours, so we compared the random seeds.
We documented the remaining difference in the experiment notes.

bad: I narrowed my research question into two directions.
good: I’ve narrowed my project down to two possible research directions.
why: Use “narrow something down to” when you reduce a project to a smaller set of options. “Research directions” names the alternatives clearly, and the present perfect connects the work you have done to the current meeting.
story: I had been reading papers to refine the focus of my dissertation.
By our meeting, I had identified two promising directions.
I told my advisor, “I’ve narrowed my research question to two possible directions.”
I summarized the evidence for each one.
My advisor asked which direction seemed more feasible with our available data.
We agreed that I would draft a short comparison before deciding.

bad: I want to discuss about my dissertation scope.
good: I’d like your advice on my dissertation scope.
why: “Discuss” takes a direct object, so it does not need “about”; “talk about” is the alternative pattern. “I’d like your advice on…” is a courteous way to signal that you want guidance on a specific decision.
story: I had drafted an outline for my dissertation proposal.
Some parts felt too broad for the time I had available.
At our meeting, I said, “I’d like your advice on my dissertation scope.”
I showed the current outline and explained which sections I was unsure about.
My advisor suggested focusing the first study on one dataset.
I revised the outline after the meeting.

bad: I’m deciding two research directions.
good: I’m deciding between two research directions.
why: Use “decide between” when choosing one option from two alternatives. The present progressive shows that the choice is still in progress, making this a clear opening for your advisor’s input.
story: I had finished reading the papers my advisor recommended.
Two research directions seemed promising for different reasons.
I explained, “I’m deciding between two research directions.”
I described the strengths and risks I saw in each option.
My advisor asked which one connected more closely to the central research question.
We agreed on a small experiment to help compare them.

bad: I made a progress on the implementation.
good: I’ve made progress on the implementation.
why: “Progress” is an uncountable noun, so it does not take “a.” The present perfect is natural for reporting work completed over a period that leads up to the current advisor meeting.
story: I had spent the week connecting the new module to our pipeline.
The basic version was running, although a few tests still failed.
I began my update by saying, “I’ve made progress on the implementation.”
I showed what worked and described the test that was still failing.
My advisor suggested checking the input format at the module boundary.
I wrote that down as my next debugging step.

bad: I have a block with the analysis.
good: I’m blocked on the analysis because I’m missing the latest data.
why: “Be blocked on” is a natural way to report work you cannot move forward on. Naming the reason helps your advisor respond with useful guidance instead of having to guess what kind of help you need.
story: I had planned to finish the analysis before our weekly meeting.
The latest data extract had not arrived, so I could not run the final comparison.
I told my advisor, “I’m blocked on the analysis because I’m missing the latest data.”
I explained what I had completed while waiting.
My advisor helped me identify a smaller check I could do with the available data.
I left with a useful task for the rest of the week.

bad: What should I prioritize to the next meeting?
good: What should I prioritize before our next meeting?
why: Use “before” to set a deadline that comes earlier than the meeting. “Prioritize” takes the work directly as its object, so the question asks which task deserves attention first.
story: We had reviewed several possible follow-up tasks for the project.
There was not enough time to complete all of them before our next check-in.
I asked, “What should I prioritize before our next meeting?”
My advisor recommended finishing the error analysis first.
We moved the lower-priority figure revision to the following week.
I updated my task list while the plan was still fresh.

bad: I want your feedback for this design choice.
good: Could I get your feedback on this design choice?
why: Use “feedback on” to introduce the work or decision you want someone to review. “Could I get…” frames the request politely, and “this design choice” points to a specific decision rather than asking for general feedback.
story: I had to choose how to divide the system into components.
I wrote down the trade-offs before our scheduled meeting.
I asked my advisor, “Could I get your feedback on this design choice?”
I explained why I had considered the two alternatives.
My advisor pointed out how one option would simplify testing.
I updated the design notes after we agreed on a direction.

bad: I’m not sure this scope can finish in my Ph.D.
good: I’m not sure this scope is feasible within my Ph.D. timeline.
why: A project scope is “feasible” if it can realistically be completed with the available time and resources. “Within my Ph.D. timeline” makes the constraint clear without saying that the scope itself can finish.
story: I had outlined three studies for my dissertation.
Each study was interesting, but the full plan seemed ambitious.
I told my advisor, “I’m not sure this scope is feasible within my Ph.D. timeline.”
We estimated the work involved in data collection and evaluation.
My advisor suggested moving one study to future work.
The revised plan felt more realistic and still addressed the main question.

bad: Can we decide a milestone in next month?
good: Could we agree on a milestone for next month?
why: “Agree on a milestone” is the usual phrasing when you and your advisor settle on a shared target. “For next month” names when the milestone is planned; “in the next month” would mean at some point during the coming month.
story: I wanted to leave our meeting with a clear short-term goal.
We had discussed several tasks but had not chosen a target date.
I asked, “Could we agree on a milestone for next month?”
My advisor suggested completing the first evaluation table.
We chose a date to review it together.
I added the milestone to my project plan.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Could you explain again?
good: Could you go over that step again?
why: “Explain again” is understandable, but it can sound abrupt and does not say what you missed. “Go over that step again” politely asks the instructor to repeat a specific part.
story: The instructor moved quickly through a proof at the board.
I understood the setup but lost track of one transformation.
I waited until there was a pause so I would not interrupt the explanation.
I raised my hand and said, “Could you go over that step again?”
The instructor repeated the transformation and named the rule being used.
I wrote the rule beside the line in my notes.
After class, I could follow the rest of the proof on my own.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: What is this?
good: What does this notation mean?
why: “What is this?” does not identify the symbol or expression, so the instructor may not know what you mean. Naming the notation makes the question clear and easy to answer.
story: A new symbol appeared in the lecture notes.
I could see how it was used, but I did not know what it represented.
I pointed to it on the slide when the instructor paused.
I asked, “What does this notation mean?”
The instructor explained that it represented a set of neighboring nodes.
I added the definition next to the symbol in my notes.
The next example made much more sense.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Why do this?
good: Why do we need this step?
why: “Why do this?” can sound impatient because it is very brief. “Why do we need this step?” clearly asks about the purpose of a particular part of a derivation or algorithm.
story: We were simplifying an expression before applying a theorem.
I could do the algebra, but I was unsure why the extra step was useful.
I wanted to understand the reasoning rather than just copy the procedure.
I asked, “Why do we need this step?”
The instructor showed that the transformation made the theorem applicable.
I noted the connection between the simplification and the theorem.
I recognized the same strategy in a later problem.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Can you give example?
good: Could you give an example of that?
why: Use “an example” with the article “an.” Adding “Could you” makes the request sound polite in a classroom, while “of that” connects it to the idea just introduced.
story: The lecture introduced the idea of a data structure invariant.
The definition sounded abstract without a concrete case.
I wanted to see how the invariant applied to an actual structure.
I asked, “Could you give an example of that?”
The instructor used a queue and traced how its invariant held after each operation.
I followed the example in my notebook.
Then I tried to construct a second example myself.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: I have a question about this equation.
good: Could you clarify what this equation represents?
why: The first sentence is grammatical and natural, but it only announces a question. If you want an explanation, asking what the equation represents tells the instructor what you need.
story: A model was written as an equation during the lecture.
I could read each term but was not sure how they fit together.
I wanted to connect the formula to the quantity being predicted.
I asked, “Could you clarify what this equation represents?”
The instructor explained what each term measured and how they related.
I labeled the terms in my notes.
The equation became easier to interpret in the next example.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Is there another way to solve?
good: Is there another way to solve this?
why: The original needs an object after “solve.” Adding “this” makes the question complete and natural when asking about another solution method.
story: We had just finished solving a system of equations by substitution.
I understood the method but wondered whether it was the only useful approach.
I wanted to compare the amount of work each method required.
I asked, “Is there another way to solve this?”
The instructor showed how elimination worked on the same system.
We compared the two methods and discussed when each was convenient.
I chose a method more confidently on the homework.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Can you explain the code line?
good: Could you explain what this line of code does?
why: “The code line” is possible but sounds less natural here; “this line of code” is the usual phrasing when pointing to a line. The question asks directly about its behavior.
story: During a programming lecture, the instructor displayed a short function.
One line used a list comprehension I had not seen before.
I pointed to the line while the class was discussing the output.
I asked, “Could you explain what this line of code does?”
The instructor broke the expression into its filtering and mapping parts.
I tested a small input by hand to check my understanding.
The pattern was easier to recognize in the next example.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Why the program return this?
good: Why does the program return this value?
why: In a direct question, use “does” before the subject and the base verb “return.” “This value” identifies what the program produced.
story: Our class traced a function with several conditional branches.
My result did not match the example output.
I checked the input and followed the path through the function again.
I asked, “Why does the program return this value?”
The instructor pointed out that one condition became true earlier than I expected.
I corrected my trace and found the branch I had missed.
Afterward, I used the same method to debug another example.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: What happen if input is empty?
good: What happens if the input is empty?
why: With the singular subject “what,” use “happens.” “The input” is a natural way to refer to the value passed to a function or program.
story: We were discussing how a function handles different inputs.
The examples all used nonempty lists.
I wondered whether the function had a special case for an empty list.
I asked, “What happens if the input is empty?”
The instructor showed that the function returned an empty result without an error.
We discussed why that behavior mattered for the caller.
I added an empty-list test to my own implementation.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Does it always work?
good: Does this approach always work?
why: “It” may be unclear when a class is comparing several methods. Naming “this approach” makes the question specific and invites discussion of its assumptions or limits.
story: The class had just seen an algorithm solve a small example.
I wondered whether the same method would work for every valid input.
I wanted to know what conditions the proof depended on.
I asked, “Does this approach always work?”
The instructor explained that the algorithm required nonnegative edge weights.
We looked at a counterexample with a negative weight.
I wrote down the condition as part of the algorithm’s assumptions.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: How we know this algorithm is correct?
good: How do we know this algorithm is correct?
why: Questions with “how” use an auxiliary verb before the subject: “How do we know…?” This phrasing asks for the reasoning or proof behind the algorithm.
story: We had studied an algorithm that selected one item at each iteration.
I could follow the steps but wanted to understand why the result was guaranteed.
The instructor had mentioned an invariant earlier in the lecture.
I asked, “How do we know this algorithm is correct?”
The instructor used the invariant to explain what remained true after every iteration.
We checked that it held initially and at termination.
I then understood how the proof supported the algorithm.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: What is difference of these?
good: What is the difference between these two methods?
why: Say “the difference between A and B,” rather than “difference of.” Naming “these two methods” also makes the comparison clear.
story: Two methods for multiplying matrices were presented in class.
Their steps looked different, but I was unsure how their costs compared.
I wanted to understand when one method would be preferable.
I asked, “What is the difference between these two methods?”
The instructor compared their assumptions and operation counts.
We discussed how matrix size affected the comparison.
I added the key distinction to my study notes.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: I don’t understand this part.
good: I’m not sure I follow this part of the proof.
why: “I don’t understand this part” is natural, but it does not identify what is confusing. The alternative narrows the issue to the proof and uses a conversational, non-confrontational phrase.
story: We were following a proof with several nested cases.
I understood the first two cases but lost the argument in the final one.
I wanted to ask about the exact point where my understanding stopped.
I said, “I’m not sure I follow this part of the proof.”
The instructor restated the goal of the final case.
That helped me see how it followed from the previous result.
I asked one more question to check the boundary condition.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Can you repeat?
good: Could you repeat the last part, please?
why: “Can you repeat?” is grammatical, but without context it can sound blunt or unclear about what should be repeated. “Could you” softens the request, and “the last part” specifies it.
story: The instructor answered a question while writing on the board.
I heard the beginning but missed the final explanation.
I waited for a pause before asking for it again.
I said, “Could you repeat the last part, please?”
The instructor repeated the explanation more slowly.
I caught the connection between the two equations.
I thanked them and continued following the lecture.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Is this answer right?
good: Could you check whether my reasoning is on the right track?
why: “Is this answer right?” is natural when checking a final answer. When you want feedback on your method, asking whether your reasoning is on the right track gives the instructor more useful context.
story: I worked through a proof exercise before class ended.
I had a result, but I was not confident about one inference.
I showed the instructor the steps I had written down.
I asked, “Could you check whether my reasoning is on the right track?”
The instructor confirmed the setup and pointed out one unsupported step.
I added a justification and checked the conclusion again.
I left knowing which part of my approach was sound.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Can you tell me the answer?
good: Could you give me a hint about how to approach this problem?
why: Asking directly for the answer can skip the learning process. If you want help getting started, asking for a hint makes that goal clear and leaves room to solve the problem yourself.
story: I was stuck on a homework problem involving recursion.
I had tried two approaches but could not see a useful base case.
I wanted guidance without being given the full solution.
I asked, “Could you give me a hint about how to approach this problem?”
The teaching assistant asked what smaller version of the problem I could solve.
That question helped me identify a suitable base case.
I finished the implementation and understood why it worked.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: What does professor mean?
good: What do you mean by “state” in this theorem?
why: In a question about meaning, include the subject with “do you mean.” Quoting the term being discussed helps the instructor identify exactly what you are asking about.
story: A theorem used the word “state” in a specific technical sense.
I knew the everyday meaning but suspected the theorem used a formal definition.
I asked while the instructor was discussing the assumptions.
I said, “What do you mean by ‘state’ in this theorem?”
The instructor defined a state as a configuration of the system at a given step.
We compared that definition with the everyday use of the word.
I understood how the term fit into the proof.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Can I ask question?
good: Could I ask a question about the last example?
why: Use “a question” with the article. In a classroom, naming the topic makes the request more useful; “Could I” is a polite way to get the floor.
story: The instructor had just finished an example of a hash table.
I had a question about what happened when two keys mapped to the same index.
I waited until the example was complete before speaking.
I asked, “Could I ask a question about the last example?”
The instructor invited me to continue.
I asked how the collision was handled in that implementation.
The answer helped me connect the example to the general strategy.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: When we use this theorem?
good: When do we use this theorem?
why: Use “do” before the subject in a present simple question: “When do we use…?” This asks about the situations where the theorem is useful.
story: A theorem appeared after a long derivation in lecture.
I understood its statement but did not know when to apply it.
I wanted to connect the theorem to the kinds of problems we were solving.
I asked, “When do we use this theorem?”
The instructor showed a problem where its conditions were satisfied.
We compared that problem with one where a condition failed.
I could recognize when the theorem might help on future assignments.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Is my understanding correct?
good: So, if I understand correctly, the running time doubles when the input size doubles?
why: The first question is natural but very broad. Restating your specific understanding lets the instructor confirm or correct the exact idea, and the question mark makes the check conversational.
story: We were discussing how input size affects an algorithm’s running time.
I thought the runtime grew linearly, but wanted to confirm the implication.
I turned the idea into a concrete statement.
I asked, “So, if I understand correctly, the running time doubles when the input size doubles?”
The instructor confirmed that this followed for a linear-time algorithm.
They contrasted it with a quadratic-time example.
I left with a clearer sense of how growth rates compare.

categoryTitle: Asking questions in computer science and math classes
bad: Why we need prove this?
good: Why do we need to prove this property?
why: In a direct question, put “do” before “we” and use the base form “need.” Adding “property” identifies what the proof is meant to establish.
story: A lecture introduced a property that seemed obvious from several examples.
I wondered why the class needed a formal proof.
I wanted to understand what examples could not guarantee.
I asked, “Why do we need to prove this property?”
The instructor explained that the claim had to hold for every valid input.
We discussed how a counterexample could expose a hidden assumption.
The proof showed the claim beyond the examples we had tested.
